slides.text: Think of cafeteria trays: every call sets a fresh tray on top, and you only ever work on the top one.
slides.alt: "Winding down: each call waits": one frame on the stack, factorial(3), waiting: 3 × ?.

slides.text: Down: factorial(3) waits on factorial(2), which waits on factorial(1), which waits on factorial(0). That's the base case: return 1.
slides.alt: Four frames stacked: factorial(0) on top marked base case → 1, then factorial(1) waiting 1 × ?, factorial(2) waiting 2 × ?, and factorial(3) waiting 3 × ? at the bottom.
"Unwinding: multiply on the way back": the stack is down to factorial(3), waiting: 3 × ?.
The stack emptied to factorial(3) = 6, with the note "4 frames = n + 1".

slides.text: return n * factorial(n - 1) # smaller problem; the multiply waits
slides.alt: Python factorial(n): if n == 0: return 1; return n * factorial(n - 1), with the last line highlighted and the note "The multiply waits until the call comes back"; the call stack shows factorial(3): 3 × 2 after factorial(2) returns 2.

slides.text: Python stops at 1,000: factorial(1000) raises "RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded". JavaScript allows around 10,000.
slides.alt: "Every frame costs memory": Python stops at 1,000 frames, factorial(1000) raises RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded; JavaScript around 10,000.

slides.text: Break the base case (step down by 2: 3 → 1 → −1 → …) and it skips 0 forever. It doesn't hang, it crashes.
slides.alt: Python broken(n): if n == 0: return 1; return n * broken(n - 2), with the last line highlighted and the note "Not a hang: a crash". The call stack piles up broken(-3), broken(-5), broken(-7), broken(-9), broken(-11): depth 8, n = −11, past 0.

challenge: how many frames deep does factorial(5) go?
